title: Semantic and episodic memory

html:
Young children’s memory abilities also improve qualitatively between ages four and five; both semantic and episodic memory show rapid development during this period as the brain’s memory systems (especially the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex) become more efficient. By age 4, children already remember plenty of factual information: for instance, a 4-year-old knows the names of many everyday objects, familiar people, perhaps some letter or number names, and so on (this is their semantic memory store). Over the next year, semantic memory expands in breadth and depth. Five-year-olds have accrued more general knowledge: they often know basic facts like the days of the week, some months, their address and phone number, and can name common coins or animals 1. They ask innumerable "Why?" and "How?" questions at this age, which fuels their semantic learning. They begin to form simple schemas and taxonomic knowledge, for example understanding that a tiger and an elephant are both animals (knowledge of categories). This is reflected in vocabulary growth and the ability to give simple definitions (e.g "what’s a fork?" -> "it’s something you eat with.").

Between four and five, episodic memory (a reflection of event modeling abilities) becomes less "gists with tags" and more truly recollective; five-year-olds bind item-context relations more reliably at encoding and retrieve those bindings after delay and interference, reflecting a shift from the retrieval limits typical at four toward recollection-based remembering. Laboratory tests that require remembering combinations (e.g., what happened with which background/room) show clear improvement from 4 to 6 years, with the biggest early gains emerging right in the preschool window 2, and follow-ups indicate that much of the four-year-old deficit is a retrieval (not encoding) bottleneck 3. Five-year-olds also show better memory for temporal order (e.g. if asked to recount the day’s events in order, a 5-year-old is more likely to correctly sequence two or three events than a 4-year-old). Source monitoring also becomes sturdier: compared to four-year-olds, five-year-olds are better at reporting where or from whom they learned something (and at keeping sources distinct), marking a step away from the "source amnesia" errors common earlier in preschool 4. Overall, the episodic memory system can (unreliably) carry out its basic functions while continuing along a steep trajectory of improvement. A 2025 study examines source-memory encoding (Figure) 12. The study analyzes an encoding-related EEG component (Figure).

These gains in episodic memory manifest in autobiographical memory; by 5, children provide more detailed and organized narratives of past events than at 3 or 4, often spontaneously including emotional or evaluative comments (e.g. "That was fun!") 5. At this age they also begin to treat "remembering" as a mental act (using verbs like "I remember..." appropriately and showing early meta-memory/subjective-recollection abilities 6, 7, 8), reflecting a growing understanding that memories are internal representations of past experiences. Consistent with that, five-year-olds can recount events from a year or more earlier 9, 10, reflecting emerging maturity of hippocampo-cortical loops.
